evaluation.positioning_hook: When a pregnant salon worker dies under impossible circumstances, a GBI agent and his partner uncover a Thai-American family, a cursed video shop, and a Krasue haunting hiding in plain sight.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The hook is immediate and genre-friendly: a dead pregnant woman, an impossible body, and a folkloric monster give the script a clean horror-mystery engine. The audience is narrower than a broad studio thriller because the Thai cultural specificity and procedural structure are the selling point, but that specificity is also the moat.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The premise lands fast through Jan’s death, the missing blood, and the later reveal of the Krasue mythology. The script is very easy to explain in two sentences, and the investigation framework gives the hook a clear forward motion.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Kim and Gaines have a workable odd-couple rhythm, and Jan/Tira/Paul/Kay all feel culturally and behaviorally specific rather than generic. The lead engine is solid, though the script is more compelling as a world and case than as a single unforgettable character showcase.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The blend of suburban Georgia procedural, Thai-American family drama, and folkloric body horror is unusually confident. The shadow-play Krasue sequence, the salon world, and the video-store detour give the script a distinct authorial stamp.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The investigation keeps generating new evidence — the cleaver, the drawing, the DVD, Tira’s apartment, the old white guy — so the script rarely stalls. The middle is more investigative than escalating, but the reveals are spaced well enough to keep the reader moving.

resonant_originality.reasoning: This feels fresh in a way that is also legible: a police case that can only be solved by understanding a specific immigrant subculture and its horror iconography. The Krasue reveal is not just decorative; it reframes the entire death in a way that feels both surprising and inevitable.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The salon, the family home, the video store, the apartment complex, and the GBI office all carry social texture and operational detail. The Thai-language household rules, salon labor dynamics, and horror-media ecosystem make the world feel story-generating rather than merely decorative.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a very specific tonal identity: procedural deadpan colliding with folkloric dread and occasional family-comedy warmth. The switch into stylized grindhouse horror is bold but still feels like part of the same piece.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There are deeper layers around grief, assimilation, fertility, and belief versus skepticism, and the old-white-guy thread hints at a wider mythology. The script shows enough surface to suggest more beneath it, though the current draft is still primarily driven by the case mechanics.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Kim/Gaines, Paul/Jan, Kay/Pranee, and the salon crew all generate usable recurring dynamics. It’s not a sprawling ensemble machine, but there are enough relationship nodes that the world can keep producing scenes.

lead_characters.name: Sue Kim
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 30s-40s, GBI senior special agent, Korean-American or Asian-American identity implied by dialogue and casting context
lead_characters.hook: A stone-faced, highly observant GBI agent who treats folklore like evidence and evidence like a language. She’s the script’s clearest audience surrogate: skeptical, dry, and increasingly convinced that the case is pointing somewhere her training doesn’t cover.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Jodie Comer in Killing Eve or Carrie Coon in The Leftovers — controlled intelligence, deadpan authority, and the slow reveal of a character whose certainty keeps getting tested. It gives an actor the pleasure of playing procedural competence while landing the quiet shock of belief.

lead_characters.name: Omar Gaines
lead_characters.hook: Kim’s partner is the more openly skeptical, more visibly reactive half of the investigative duo, with a comic physicality that keeps him human inside the procedural machinery. He’s the guy who can roll his eyes at a floating-head vampire and still become the audience’s entry point into the weirdness.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of partner role that gave Walton Goggins in Justified or Jesse Plemons in Fargo room to be funny, grounded, and slowly unnerved. It’s a strong character-actor part with real scene-stealing opportunities in the banter and the disbelief.

lead_characters.name: Jansuda Phongphat
lead_characters.demographics: Female, late teens to early 20s, Thai-American, salon worker, pregnant
lead_characters.hook: Jan is the emotional center of the tragedy: young, exhausted, private, and visibly carrying more than she says. Her silence, hesitation, and final isolation make her death feel personal before it becomes supernatural.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Riley Keough in The Girlfriend Experience or Jena Malone in Don’t Let Go a chance to play interiority under pressure. Even with limited page time, it offers a strong emotional before-and-after and a haunting physical transformation.

lead_characters.name: Pattapol Srisuk
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 40s, Thai-American, salon worker, family driver and connector
lead_characters.hook: Paul is the social lubricant of the family and salon, a stylish, affectionate, slightly performative uncle/cousin figure who can move between Thai and English with ease. He’s funny, affectionate, and more important than he first appears, because he knows everyone and everything in the ecosystem.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do what Bobby Cannavale did in Boardwalk Empire or Randall Park does in ensemble comedy-drama: charm, authority, and a little mystery. It’s a scene-rich supporting part with enough personality to become memorable fast.

lead_characters.name: Kanokwan Phongphat
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 60s, Thai-American, salon owner / family matriarch
lead_characters.hook: Kay is the household’s moral center and disciplinary force, stern about language, work, and emotional discipline. She reads as practical and unsentimental, but the script lets her warmth show through in the way she manages the family and the salon.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of matriarch role that gave Margo Martindale in The Americans or Hong Chau in The Whale real authority and emotional weight. It offers an actor command, restraint, and the chance to play a woman whose toughness is also her love language.

lead_characters.name: Pranee Srisuk
lead_characters.demographics: Female, late 20s, Thai-American, mother, salon worker
lead_characters.hook: Pranee is the more openly emotional family member, balancing domestic labor, motherhood, and the social pressure of the household. She’s observant and reactive, with enough skepticism and tenderness to keep scenes alive around her.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of grounded family role that gave Melanie Lynskey in Yellowjackets or Aunjanue Ellis-Taylor in King Richard room to be both practical and emotionally porous. It’s a strong supporting part with maternal specificity and real reaction work.

lead_characters.name: Chanthira Boonmee
lead_characters.demographics: Female, mid-30s, Thai or Thai-American, salon worker
lead_characters.hook: Tira is the script’s most volatile supporting presence: withdrawn, grief-struck, and then suddenly alarming in a way that suggests she’s already halfway into another reality. She’s written as a mystery before she becomes a corpse, which gives the role eerie momentum.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Rebecca Hall in Resurrection or Mia Goth in Pearl a chance to pivot from wounded realism into full-body horror. It’s a transformation part with a strong emotional and physical payoff.

lead_characters.name: Chai Srisuk
lead_characters.hook: Chai is the absent husband whose normality becomes suspicious by proximity to the case. He’s polished, corporate, and emotionally constrained, which makes him useful as a pressure point in the family dynamic.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor play polished surface with a crack underneath, similar to what John Cho brought to Columbus or what Steven Yeun can do in a contained dramatic scene. It’s a clean, credible supporting part with latent tension.

lead_characters.name: Emily Ortiz
lead_characters.hook: Ortiz is the sharper, more openly skeptical forensic presence in the room, and the script gives her just enough personality to register as more than process. She’s the one who can puncture the room with a line and still feel like she belongs in the machinery.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the dry authority of a procedural regular, like what Sarah Steele or Aya Cash can do in ensemble work. It’s a compact but useful part with attitude and competence.

lead_characters.name: Ryan Patel
lead_characters.hook: Patel is the quieter support player who helps widen the procedural world and gives the GBI scenes a lived-in office texture. He’s not flashy, but he makes the investigation feel staffed by real people.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the steady utility of a smart ensemble player, like what Kumail Nanjiani or Utkarsh Ambudkar can do in grounded procedural work. It’s a credible, low-friction supporting part.

lead_characters.name: Joe Reese
lead_characters.hook: Reese is the authority figure who has to absorb the weirdness and keep the room moving. He’s a classic procedural boss role: calm, skeptical, and increasingly cornered by the evidence.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the gravitas of a Michael McKean or Clark Gregg type in a procedural ensemble. It’s a clean authority part with a few good reaction beats.

lead_characters.name: Vic Lacayo
lead_characters.hook: Vic is the exhausted gatekeeper to the horror-media underworld, a guy who knows the inventory and the subculture better than anyone else in the room. He gives the script a lived-in, slightly grimy texture that broadens the world beyond the salon and the family home.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the offbeat specificity of a character part in a Coen-adjacent ensemble. It’s small but memorable, with a nice comic-dry edge.

lead_characters.name: Jaz Carter
lead_characters.demographics: Female, early 20s, Black, video store clerk
lead_characters.hook: Jaz is the coolest person in the room, bored, stylish, and casually encyclopedic about international horror. She’s a quick-hit supporting character who instantly makes the world feel younger and more culturally connected.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do sharp, low-effort cool in the mold of a Natasha Lyonne side character or a Zazie Beetz scene-stealer. It’s brief but highly legible.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: theatrical specialty or streaming-first genre launch

budget.note: Contemporary and mostly interior, but the Krasue sequence, corpse makeup, blood effects, and stylized horror finale will push above a simple contained-drama cost profile.

casting.note: The project needs a credible Thai-American ensemble with bilingual performance ability, plus a lead who can play deadpan procedural authority and escalating disbelief.

development.note: The script’s appeal depends on balancing procedural clarity with folkloric specificity; the old-white-guy thread and the Krasue reveal need to stay legible to buyers outside the cultural context.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adult genre viewers who like smart horror with cultural specificity, procedural structure, and a strong female investigator.
audience_target.demographics: 25-54, slightly female-skewing, urban/coastal and streamer-native, with strong appeal to Asian-American audiences and horror fans who like folklore-driven material.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary Atlanta locations keep the base cost contained, while creature effects, gore, night work, and a few stylized horror set pieces push it above microbudget.

types_of_buyers: streamer original film teams building elevated-horror slates
lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane where cultural specificity is the selling point, not a barrier. The script has enough procedural clarity for mainstream genre buyers and enough mythic texture for prestige horror buyers.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature. The world is rich, but the script does not yet present a clean sequel or spinoff vector with a separate anchor character.

strengths.what_it_means: The script turns a specific monster mythology into a commercial mystery structure, which makes the supernatural feel investigable rather than abstract. That is the kind of hook that can travel to buyers who want elevated horror with a clean narrative spine.
strengths.evidence: The missing blood, the salon DVD, the floating-head lore, and the forensic conference all point to the same reveal path.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Kim is a strong buyer-facing lead.
strengths.what_it_means: A deadpan investigator who can carry both skepticism and eventual belief is a very marketable anchor for genre material. That role gives a platform to an actor who can play authority, wit, and dawning dread in the same frame.
strengths.evidence: Her reactions to the floating-head story, the video-store discovery, and the final monitor reveal all land cleanly.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The Thai-American family world feels lived-in.
strengths.what_it_means: The salon/home ecosystem gives the script a textured social world that can support both emotional investment and production value. Buyers respond to worlds that feel specific enough to generate scenes, not just plot points.
strengths.evidence: The Thai/English household rules, salon labor, family hierarchy, and video-store horror subculture all feel distinct.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The horror reveal is visually ownable.
strengths.what_it_means: The shadow-play Krasue sequence gives the project a signature set piece that can sell the movie in a trailer and in a pitch room. It’s the kind of sequence that tells a buyer the film has a point of view, not just a premise.
strengths.evidence: The shoji-screen shadow play, the floating head, the entrails, and the dawn ash sequence are all highly imageable.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The procedural banter broadens the audience.
strengths.what_it_means: The Kim/Gaines dynamic keeps the script from becoming pure folklore exposition and gives it a more accessible, mainstream entry point. That helps the movie play to both horror fans and viewers who want character chemistry.
strengths.evidence: Their loafers joke, the DVD skepticism, and the old-white-guy reveal all play as dry procedural comedy.

whats_special.headline: This is a smart, culturally specific horror mystery with a real commercial spine: a deadpan GBI lead, a folkloric creature reveal, and a world that feels both fresh and filmable. The contained contemporary setting keeps the economics in indie range while the Krasue imagery and procedural structure give buyers a clear trailer, festival, and streaming lane.

items.area: The lead is more observer than driver.
items.detail: Kim is compelling as a skeptical investigator, but the script’s emotional center sits more in the case than in her personal life. That makes the role strong for casting and procedural momentum, but it also means the buyer conversation will focus on concept execution more than character franchise value.

items.area: The cultural mythology needs buyer-side translation.
items.detail: The Krasue, kuman thong, and luk thep material is vivid, but it’s also highly specific and can read as opaque without the right framing. For some buyers, that specificity is the asset; for others, it becomes a development question about how much explanation the audience will need.

items.area: The procedural middle is more investigative than escalating.
items.detail: The salon visit, the video-store detour, and the apartment discovery are all useful, but they function as accumulation more than a hard turn. That keeps the script coherent, though it also means the momentum depends on the novelty of each clue rather than on a strong external clock.

items.area: The music and brand footprint needs cleanup.
items.detail: The draft names multiple songs and brands — including Rhymekhamhaeng, Ramintra, Udom Silapin na Chiang Mai, Chaweewan Dumern, Gucci, Venmo, Ring, Fanta, AWS, and Kiwi. Those are manageable individually, but together they create a real clearance and budget conversation before greenlight.

issues.headline: The script’s main friction is not the premise; it’s the balance between a culturally specific supernatural mythology and the more familiar procedural frame around it. Buyers will also notice that the lead role is strongest as an investigator, not as a deeply personal engine, so the project lives or dies on concept execution and the right cast.
